story.title: Colonization of India: trade, conquest, resistance and independence in 140 moments
story.introHtml:
European power grew through trade, fortified ports, treaties, taxation and conquest. These short, sourced moments follow resistance through regional wars, collective refusal, constitutional politics, nonviolent campaigns and revolutionary action.

The main sequence reaches independence and Partition in 1947. A brief epilogue follows the Republic and the remaining European enclaves through 1962. Sources identify the perspectives of officials, rebels and participants, including later memoirs.

chapters.title: An existing ocean economy
chapters.html: Indian merchants, ports and producers already traded with East Africa, Arabia and Southeast Asia. European newcomers entered these networks and negotiated with established rulers; they did not create India’s overseas commerce. [1]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: Da Gama reaches Calicut
chapters.html: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 through the sea route around Africa. His expedition sought access to Asian markets, encountering an established commercial world on the Malabar coast. [1]

image.alt: Later artwork · Vasco da Gama
image.caption: Later artwork · Vasco da Gama
image.author: Oskar Freiwirth-Lützow

chapters.title: Negotiating access ashore
chapters.html: The voyage journal records commercial expectations, misunderstandings and friction with established merchants. A sea route gave Portugal access to Asian markets, but trading ashore still required Indian political relationships. [1]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: Trade backed by naval violence
chapters.html: Da Gama’s second voyage used force to demand commercial advantages. Gaspar Correia’s later Portuguese chronicle describes attacks on shipping and the destruction of a pilgrim vessel. [2]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: The conquest of Goa
chapters.html: Albuquerque captured Goa, lost it and retook it in 1510. Portuguese fleets and soldiers worked with Indian allies to establish a fortified territorial foothold. [3]

image.alt: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.caption: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.author: Assamtimes

chapters.title: Goa becomes an imperial centre
chapters.html: Goa became an administrative and commercial centre of the Estado da Índia. Its fortified base supported a wider Portuguese network within a much larger Indian political landscape. [3]

image.alt: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.caption: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.author: Assamtimes

chapters.title: A network of fortified ports
chapters.html: The conquests of Malacca and Hormuz linked Portuguese positions around India with strategic sea passages. Forts and fleets sought to direct commerce, although maritime control remained uneven. [3]

image.alt: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.caption: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.author: Assamtimes

chapters.title: Missions and royal authority
chapters.html: Francis Xavier’s letters sought support from the Portuguese crown and its officers for religious conversion. Missionary projects accompanied colonial trade and warfare, bringing religious pressure into encounters with local communities. [4]

image.alt: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.caption: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.author: Assamtimes

chapters.title: The English company is chartered
chapters.html: Elizabeth I incorporated the English East India Company on 31 December 1600. Its royal charter granted a trading monopoly over an immense eastern area claimed in English law. [5]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: A charter was not Indian sovereignty
chapters.html: The English charter authorised a corporation within English law. Its monopoly did not itself give the company sovereignty over Indian rulers and populations with whom it would trade. [5]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: A Dutch company competes
chapters.html: The VOC received its charter in 1602, with powers to make agreements and maintain armed establishments. Dutch factories relied on Asian goods, labour, credit and political negotiation. [6]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: English merchants at Surat
chapters.html: English merchants established a factory at Surat. It was a trading establishment whose access, customs arrangements and protection depended on negotiation with Indian authorities. [5]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: Roe seeks imperial protection
chapters.html: Thomas Roe sought favourable conditions from Jahangir’s court. His journal and company correspondence describe negotiations over customs, access and protection for merchants operating under Mughal authority. [5]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The Tranquebar treaty
chapters.html: Raghunatha Nayak of Thanjavur permitted a Danish settlement and fort at Tarangambadi. The treaty and Jon Ólafsson’s account record a negotiated beginning for this smaller European establishment. [6]

image.alt: Historical document · The Tranquebar treaty · 1620
image.caption: Historical document · The Tranquebar treaty · 1620
image.author: Unknown

chapters.title: Madras and Fort St George
chapters.html: A Coromandel grant enabled the English to establish Madras and Fort St George. Local merchants, textile producers and intermediaries sustained the trade behind the growing fortified settlement. [5]

image.alt: Historical print · Fort St George, Madras · 1754
image.caption: Historical print · Fort St George, Madras · 1754
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: Bombay passes between crowns
chapters.html: The Portuguese-English royal marriage settlement transferred Bombay to the English crown. Turning the diplomatic agreement into possession and administration proved difficult, as company records show. [5]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: A French foothold
chapters.html: The French East India Company was founded in 1664. Pondicherry grew as a major settlement from the 1670s, adding another European competitor for commerce and political influence. [7]

image.alt: Map · Pondicherry and its surroundings
image.caption: Map · Pondicherry and its surroundings
image.author: Leveux, M.

chapters.title: Bombay is leased to the company
chapters.html: The English crown leased Bombay to the East India Company in 1668. The harbour strengthened its western position, with commercial importance growing through later investment and expansion. [5]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Mughal power checks the company
chapters.html: The English company’s attempt to use force against Mughal authority failed. Restoring trade required renewed negotiation with an imperial government it could not yet overcome. [5]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: Calcutta and imperial privileges
chapters.html: Company settlements developed around Calcutta. Farrukhsiyar’s 1717 farman confirmed important trading privileges, creating advantages whose interpretation would become a source of conflict with Bengal’s government. [5]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Privileges become political disputes
chapters.html: Customs exemptions, private trade and the protection of company establishments became political questions in Bengal. Disputes over privileges preceded the company’s later territorial conquest. [5]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: The Carnatic Wars
chapters.html: English and French forces backed rival Indian claimants and negotiated regional alliances. Warfare depended on finance and fortified settlements; English victories weakened France’s position in southern India. [7]

image.alt: Map · Pondicherry and its surroundings
image.caption: Map · Pondicherry and its surroundings
image.author: Leveux, M.

chapters.title: Plassey changes Bengal’s politics
chapters.html: Clive’s forces defeated Siraj ud-Daulah at Plassey on 23 June 1757. The victory opened Bengal’s government to deeper company intervention, rather than bringing all India under British rule. [8]

image.alt: Later artwork · Clive and Mir Jafar after Plassey
image.caption: Later artwork · Clive and Mir Jafar after Plassey
image.author: Francis Hayman

chapters.title: Allies behind the battlefield
chapters.html: Clive negotiated with opponents of Siraj ud-Daulah, including Mir Jafar. These political agreements were central to Plassey; Clive’s letters celebrate the outcome from the victor’s perspective. [8]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Victory at Buxar
chapters.html: The company defeated the coalition involving Mir Qasim, Shuja ud-Daula and Shah Alam II in 1764. Subsequent treaties converted military success into stronger political leverage across the Gangetic plain. [8,9]

image.alt: Later artwork · The grant of the diwani
image.caption: Later artwork · The grant of the diwani
image.author: Benjamin West

chapters.title: The diwani grant
chapters.html: Shah Alam II granted the company revenue-collecting authority over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765. A trading corporation now gained access to the income of extensive Indian territories. [9,11]

image.alt: Later artwork · The grant of the diwani
image.caption: Later artwork · The grant of the diwani
image.author: Benjamin West

chapters.title: Revenue sustains military power
chapters.html: Tax income could finance armies and government as well as commerce. Administrative records show the coercive work behind revenue collection, rather than an effortless transition to uniform rule. [9,11]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: Mysore resists expansion
chapters.html: Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan fought the company through wars, alliances and diplomacy. Mysore’s military resources and foreign partnerships challenged company expansion within a wider contest among Indian powers. [12]

image.alt: Later artwork · Tipu Sultan
image.caption: Later artwork · Tipu Sultan
image.author: Anonymous

chapters.title: The Bengal famine
chapters.html: Crop failure, high prices and a company-directed revenue system accompanied Bengal’s devastating famine. Company correspondence and parliamentary inquiries record suffering beneath the expansion of colonial fiscal power. [11]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Parliament intervenes
chapters.html: Financial troubles and accusations about company conduct prompted parliamentary action. The Regulating Act reorganised Indian government and established a governor-general in Bengal. [10]

image.alt: Later artwork · The grant of the diwani
image.caption: Later artwork · The grant of the diwani
image.author: Benjamin West

chapters.title: A Supreme Court is established
chapters.html: The Regulating Act created a Supreme Court at Calcutta. Its relationship with the reorganised government generated jurisdictional disputes, exposing tensions within the company’s new governing arrangements. [10]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The Treaty of Salbai
chapters.html: The First Anglo-Maratha War ended with the Treaty of Salbai in 1782. Maratha power forced negotiation, interrupting company ambitions and demonstrating that expansion faced consequential reverses. [9]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Pitt’s India Act
chapters.html: A Board of Control brought company political affairs under closer British state supervision. Directors and shareholders retained influence, but corporate government became increasingly tied to metropolitan policy. [10]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: Pazhassi Raja’s resistance
chapters.html: Pazhassi Raja and his supporters resisted company demands in Malabar’s forests and hills. Local communities sustained the struggle; his death in 1805 ended a leading role. [13]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The Permanent Settlement
chapters.html: Regulation I of 1793 fixed the government’s assessed revenue demand upon participating zamindars. The arrangement strengthened a particular form of landed property in Bengal. [11]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: A fixed assessment, insecure tenants
chapters.html: Permanence applied to the government’s assessment upon zamindars. It did not guarantee cultivators secure land or prosperity: tenants still faced demands, disputes and vulnerability. [11]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Subsidiary alliances
chapters.html: Indian rulers supporting British-controlled forces accepted fiscal obligations and limits on diplomacy and military independence. Treaty arrangements extended company power without immediately annexing every subordinated state. [9,12]

image.alt: Later artwork · The grant of the diwani
image.caption: Later artwork · The grant of the diwani
image.author: Benjamin West

chapters.title: Tipu Sultan’s final battle
chapters.html: Tipu Sultan died when company and allied forces stormed Srirangapatna in May 1799. The victory removed a major opponent of British expansion in southern India. [12]

image.alt: Map · Srirangapatna · 1799
image.caption: Map · Srirangapatna · 1799
image.author: Anonymous

chapters.title: A kingdom survives under restrictions
chapters.html: The postwar settlement divided territory and restored a Wodeyar ruler under restrictive conditions. Company influence expanded through a new political arrangement after the destruction of Tipu’s government. [12]

image.alt: Later artwork · Tipu Sultan
image.caption: Later artwork · Tipu Sultan
image.author: Anonymous

chapters.title: The Poligar Wars
chapters.html: Kattabomman, the Marudhu brothers and other poligars resisted demands over tribute, military power and local authority. Company campaigns brought executions and the dismantling of fortified positions. [13]

image.alt: Historical print · Fort St George, Madras · 1754
image.caption: Historical print · Fort St George, Madras · 1754
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.date: Early nineteenth century · Different revenue regions
chapters.title: Revenue from individual cultivators
chapters.html: Ryotwari arrangements assessed individual cultivators in important southern and western regions. Colonial land taxation developed through different provincial systems rather than one uniform settlement. [11]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Village-based revenue assessments
chapters.html: Mahalwari settlements assessed revenue through villages or estates in parts of northern India. Official minutes and parliamentary evidence record the arguments behind this distinct arrangement. [11]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Maratha supremacy is broken
chapters.html: Later Anglo-Maratha wars combined military conquest with imposed treaties. Company victories weakened the major Maratha powers and ended the peshwa’s rule in 1818. [9,12]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Trading monopolies are dismantled
chapters.html: The Charter Acts progressively removed the company’s commercial monopolies. Parliamentary settlements opened India further to other British business interests while changing the corporation’s legal role. [10]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: The Paika uprising
chapters.html: Bakshi Jagabandhu’s uprising drew together groups affected by conquest and changes in Odisha’s revenue, landholding and authority. Official correspondence records resistance and the colonial response. [13]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Protection under British supremacy
chapters.html: Mewar’s treaty of 13 January 1818 acknowledged British supremacy while preserving internal hereditary government. Protection agreements could therefore subordinate a state without turning it immediately into annexed territory. [9]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Indirect rule after conquest
chapters.html: Some Maratha ruling houses survived within a subordinate order. Military dispatches and settlements show how imposed agreements could preserve local dynasties while extending colonial political control. [9,12]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The prohibition of sati
chapters.html: The Bengal regulation prohibiting sati changed colonial law in 1829. The measure followed Indian arguments over the practice and became part of a contested field of reform. [14]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Indian arguments over reform
chapters.html: Rammohan Roy had argued against sati, while other Indian petitioners opposed prohibition. Contemporary writings reveal an active Indian debate alongside the colonial government’s legal intervention. [14]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Indentured labour crosses oceans
chapters.html: Recruitment under indenture carried Indian workers to plantations and other colonial workplaces overseas. These migrations connected India to a wider imperial labour system and formed enduring diaspora communities. [14]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: Contracts and constrained freedom
chapters.html: Contracts, inquiries and migrants’ testimony describe disputed recruitment, demanding work and restrictions on freedom. Racial exclusion overseas also shaped the political organising of Indian diaspora communities. [14]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: The Kol uprising
chapters.html: Communities in Chotanagpur confronted changing land control, revenue demands and outsiders’ power. The uprising challenged the social order emerging under colonial administration and faced military repression. [13]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: A government without a trading business
chapters.html: The 1833 settlement ended the company’s commercial role but retained its administrative authority. Parliamentary records distinguish this governing institution from the privileged trading corporation of earlier centuries. [10]

image.alt: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.caption: Later artwork · East India Company ships
image.author: Unknown artist (British school)

chapters.title: Macaulay’s education argument
chapters.html: Macaulay’s Minute promoted English education while disparaging Indian and Arabic learning. Its assumptions about cultural authority influenced colonial policy; Indians also used English education to criticise imperial rule. [14]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The conquest of Punjab
chapters.html: Two Anglo-Sikh wars ended in the company’s annexation of Punjab in 1849. Treaties, dispatches and proclamations record the transition from negotiated relations to direct colonial administration. [15]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The Doctrine of Lapse
chapters.html: The company refused to recognise certain adopted heirs as successors to sovereignty and annexed several states. Dispossession and lost dynastic rights generated grievances that later shaped resistance. [15]

image.alt: Later artwork · Lakshmibai of Jhansi
image.caption: Later artwork · Lakshmibai of Jhansi
image.author: Unknown artist

chapters.title: An existing state is displaced
chapters.html: Annexation ended the Sikh kingdom’s sovereignty and displaced its young ruler, Duleep Singh. British proclamations presented the takeover through claims of order and administrative necessity. [15]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Railways and imperial priorities
chapters.html: Railways transformed transport and economic relationships. Government guarantees and military requirements shaped investment, linking infrastructure to commerce and colonial control as well as passenger travel. [21,22]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Who paid for the railways?
chapters.html: Parliamentary evidence and Indian critics examined railway costs, returns and priorities. The benefits of improved transport did not resolve questions about who financed, controlled or profited from the system. [21,22]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Dadabhai Naoroji · 1892
image.caption: Historical photograph · Dadabhai Naoroji · 1892
image.author: R.M. Richardson & Co

chapters.title: The Santal Hul
chapters.html: Sidhu and Kanhu led an uprising against exploitation involving moneylenders, landlords, police and the colonial order. Official correspondence records the scale of the challenge and military repression. [16]

image.alt: Historical print · Sidhu, in a colonial-period illustration · 1856
image.caption: Historical print · Sidhu, in a colonial-period illustration · 1856
image.author: Illustrated London News

chapters.title: Awadh is annexed
chapters.html: The company annexed Awadh on grounds of alleged misgovernment and removed Wajid Ali Shah. British official papers presented their justification for displacing an existing political authority. [15]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The social consequences of annexation
chapters.html: The change affected court dependants, landholders, soldiers and cultivators. These disruptions help explain Awadh’s intense resistance in 1857, alongside the grievances surrounding military service. [15]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Meerut and Delhi rise
chapters.html: Sepoys at Meerut rose on 10 May 1857. Reaching Delhi the following day, rebels sought Bahadur Shah Zafar’s authority as the military revolt widened into a political crisis. [17,18]

image.alt: Map · Delhi during the uprising · 1857
image.caption: Map · Delhi during the uprising · 1857
image.author: Unknown

chapters.title: A widening field of grievances
chapters.html: Religion, pay, land and political authority shaped participation in the uprising. Changing military and civilian alliances spread the crisis, while regions and communities made different choices. [17,18]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: A rebel proclamation
chapters.html: The Azamgarh Proclamation appealed to landholders, merchants, officials, artisans and religious figures. It promised remedies against British rule and invoked joint Hindu-Muslim action, expressing one rebel programme. [17]

image.alt: Map · Delhi during the uprising · 1857
image.caption: Map · Delhi during the uprising · 1857
image.author: Unknown

chapters.title: Begum Hazrat Mahal’s resistance
chapters.html: Begum Hazrat Mahal sustained resistance in Awadh in her son Birjis Qadr’s name. Her response to Victoria’s proclamation challenged British assurances rather than accepting the new Crown settlement. [17,18]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Atrocities and reprisals
chapters.html: Rebel forces killed civilians, while British reprisals included executions and attacks on communities. Correspondence and participant memoirs record violence against people caught on different sides of the conflict. [18]

image.alt: Map · Delhi during the uprising · 1857
image.caption: Map · Delhi during the uprising · 1857
image.author: Unknown

chapters.title: Lakshmibai’s final campaigns
chapters.html: Lakshmibai fought around Jhansi, Kalpi and Gwalior after the loss of Jhansi’s sovereignty. She died in June 1858 as the rebellion faced British reconquest. [18]

image.alt: Later artwork · Lakshmibai of Jhansi
image.caption: Later artwork · Lakshmibai of Jhansi
image.author: Unknown artist

chapters.title: Company rule ends
chapters.html: The Government of India Act transferred company government to the British Crown in 1858. Imperial authority continued through a changed governing structure after the uprising. [19]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Victoria’s proclamation
chapters.html: The proclamation promised religious protection, respect for certain princely rights and impartial legal treatment. These official commitments coexisted with continuing racial hierarchy and political exclusion under colonial rule. [19]

image.alt: Map · Delhi during the uprising · 1857
image.caption: Map · Delhi during the uprising · 1857
image.author: Unknown

chapters.title: Indigo cultivators refuse
chapters.html: Bengal cultivators collectively resisted coercive indigo contracts and European planters’ pressures. Organisation and public controversy helped force an inquiry, whose evidence recorded grievances and the operation of coercion. [20]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.date: Late nineteenth century · Indian economic criticism
chapters.title: Naoroji’s drain argument
chapters.html: Dadabhai Naoroji argued that remittances, official employment and imperial financial arrangements transferred resources out of India. His calculations and speeches made economic criticism part of the demand for political power. [21]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Dadabhai Naoroji · 1892
image.caption: Historical photograph · Dadabhai Naoroji · 1892
image.author: R.M. Richardson & Co

chapters.title: Famine relief and responsibility
chapters.html: Repeated famines brought commissions and relief rules. Their reports examined food access, employment and transport alongside harvest failure, while Indian critics challenged the adequacy of government action. [22]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Restrictions on Indian-language newspapers
chapters.html: The Vernacular Press Act expanded government control over Indian-language publications deemed dangerous. Editors challenged unequal treatment as newspapers became instruments of political organisation and targets of colonial restriction. [23]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The first Congress session
chapters.html: The Indian National Congress first met in Bombay in December 1885. Continuing meetings created an organisation in which political demands could be debated across regions. [24]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.caption: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: Reform before complete independence
chapters.html: Early Congress delegates sought administrative reform, wider representation and changes in public employment and expenditure. Complete independence was not yet their declared programme. [24]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Dadabhai Naoroji · 1892
image.caption: Historical photograph · Dadabhai Naoroji · 1892
image.author: R.M. Richardson & Co

chapters.title: Birsa Munda and Ulgulan
chapters.html: Birsa’s movement combined religious renewal with opposition to lost customary rights, landlords, missionaries and colonial authority. Ulgulan brought armed confrontation and severe repression in the Munda country. [25]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Swadeshi and boycott
chapters.html: Bengal’s partition provoked meetings, boycott of imported goods and promotion of Indian production. Daily consumption became political, while disagreements over methods and participation accompanied surveillance and repression. [24,26]

image.alt: Map · The partition of Bengal · 1905
image.caption: Map · The partition of Bengal · 1905
image.author: XrysD

chapters.title: Self-government at Congress
chapters.html: Naoroji’s Congress presidential address placed self-government at the centre of political aspiration. Debates over swaraj developed alongside changing organisations and competing claims to political representation. [21,24]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Dadabhai Naoroji · 1892
image.caption: Historical photograph · Dadabhai Naoroji · 1892
image.author: R.M. Richardson & Co

chapters.title: The Muslim League is founded
chapters.html: The All-India Muslim League introduced another organisation making constitutional claims. Cooperation, competition and changing definitions of representation would shape its relations with Congress over subsequent decades. [24,39]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The Surat split
chapters.html: The Congress session broke down over leadership, tactics and organisation. Groups called moderates and extremists contested political direction, although neither label described a permanently uniform camp. [24]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.caption: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: The Muzaffarpur bombing
chapters.html: Revolutionary organisations pursued attacks on colonial officials. The Muzaffarpur bombing killed two women who were not the intended target, exposing the human consequences of clandestine political violence. [26]

image.alt: Map · The partition of Bengal · 1905
image.caption: Map · The partition of Bengal · 1905
image.author: XrysD

chapters.title: The Alipore proceedings
chapters.html: The Alipore case became a major trial of revolutionary networks. The later Sedition Committee report preserves the colonial administration’s account of organisations it sought to suppress. [26]

image.alt: Map · The partition of Bengal · 1905
image.caption: Map · The partition of Bengal · 1905
image.author: XrysD

chapters.title: Councils and separate electorates
chapters.html: The Indian Councils Act enlarged legislative councils and introduced separate Muslim electorates. Limited representation opened political opportunities while retaining imperial control and making community representation increasingly contested. [27]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Gandhi’s Hind Swaraj
chapters.html: Gandhi argued that replacing British rulers alone would not deliver his vision of freedom. He connected self-rule with self-discipline, ethics and criticism of modern civilisation. [28]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1912
image.caption: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1912
image.author: Anonymous

chapters.title: Ghadar calls for revolt
chapters.html: Ghadar activists organised among migrants, especially in North America. Their newspaper advocated the armed overthrow of British rule, while colonial intelligence followed and attempted to suppress the movement. [26]

image.alt: Historical print · The Ghadar newspaper · 1913
image.caption: Historical print · The Ghadar newspaper · 1913
image.author: Ghadar Party

chapters.title: From overseas exclusion to rebellion
chapters.html: Ghadar networks linked racial exclusion overseas with plans for rebellion and military defections in India. Their newspaper supplies a public voice distinct from the colonial intelligence record. [26]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: India in the First World War
chapters.html: British India supplied soldiers, money and material for the war. Emergency restrictions strengthened government powers, while revolutionary groups sought openings and expectations of political reform grew. [26,27]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The Home Rule leagues
chapters.html: Annie Besant and Bal Gangadhar Tilak promoted Home Rule through leagues, meetings and political education. Organised campaigning pressed the demand for self-government during the war. [24]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.caption: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: Congress and the League agree
chapters.html: Congress and the Muslim League reached agreement on constitutional demands and representation. Their resolutions showed negotiated cooperation alongside unresolved questions about self-government and the distribution of power. [24]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.caption: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: Champaran satyagraha
chapters.html: Gandhi investigated indigo cultivators’ grievances and refused an order to leave. His account emphasises testimony, organisation and practical work that connected a local agrarian struggle with resistance to authority. [28]

image.alt: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.caption: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.author: Nizil Shah

chapters.title: Kheda’s tax refusal
chapters.html: The Kheda campaign opposed revenue collection during agricultural distress. Gandhi’s account presents collective refusal as an experiment in disciplined nonviolent action arising from a specific rural conflict. [28]

image.alt: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.caption: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.author: Nizil Shah

chapters.title: A textile workers’ strike
chapters.html: The Ahmedabad dispute concerned wages and industrial relations. Gandhi’s account presents the strike as another demanding experiment in collective discipline, distinct from the agrarian campaign at Kheda. [28]

image.alt: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.caption: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.author: Nizil Shah

chapters.title: Protest against the Rowlatt laws
chapters.html: Wartime-style restrictions continued through the Rowlatt legislation. Gandhi called for satyagraha; hartals and demonstrations spread, with violence and repression in some places challenging the movement’s discipline. [26,29]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre
chapters.html: Dyer ordered firing on a gathering at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919. The inquiry and his testimony document the act and the justification offered by those responsible. [30]

image.alt: Historic site · Mahatma Gandhi
image.caption: Historic site · Mahatma Gandhi
image.author: Bernard Gagnon

chapters.title: Tagore renounces his knighthood
chapters.html: Tagore rejected his knighthood in response to the humiliation and violence at Amritsar. His letter records an Indian answer to the imperial justification of repression. [30]

image.alt: Historic site · Mahatma Gandhi
image.caption: Historic site · Mahatma Gandhi
image.author: Bernard Gagnon

chapters.title: Dyarchy divides provincial power
chapters.html: The Government of India Act separated provincial subjects administered by ministers from those retained under official control. New political arenas opened without a transfer of sovereignty. [27]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The non-cooperation programme
chapters.html: Congress called for rejection of honours, withdrawal from institutions and promotion of swadeshi and khadi. Gandhi insisted on nonviolence as the campaign drew wider participation and varied local grievances. [24,29]

image.alt: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.caption: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.author: Nizil Shah

chapters.title: Khilafat and mass participation
chapters.html: The Khilafat issue helped mobilise many Muslims within non-cooperation. Participants brought different local concerns, creating tensions between national instructions, collective discipline and action on the ground. [24,29]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1912
image.caption: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1912
image.author: Anonymous

chapters.title: The Malabar rebellion
chapters.html: Agrarian tensions and Khilafat mobilisation fed armed confrontation with the state. The rebellion also included attacks on civilians and religious coercion, followed by severe colonial repression. [31]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Chauri Chaura and suspension
chapters.html: A clash at Chauri Chaura ended with a police station burned and policemen killed. Gandhi suspended the planned mass campaign, judging that the necessary nonviolent discipline was lacking. [29]

image.alt: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.caption: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.author: Nizil Shah

chapters.title: Councils and constructive work
chapters.html: The Swaraj Party sought to challenge government through legislative councils. Other Congress workers pursued constructive programmes and organisation outside them, sustaining politics between nationwide campaigns. [24,29]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.caption: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: The Kakori action
chapters.html: Hindustan Republican Association members took government money from a train near Kakori. A passenger was killed during the action, which brought a major prosecution of the revolutionary organisation. [32]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Ram Prasad Bismil
image.caption: Historical photograph · Ram Prasad Bismil
image.author: Uttar Pradesh state archives

chapters.title: The Kakori trial and sentences
chapters.html: The prosecution led to executions and long prison sentences. Participants’ prison writings and court records preserve different accounts of the action’s motives and responsibilities. [32]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Ram Prasad Bismil
image.caption: Historical photograph · Ram Prasad Bismil
image.author: Uttar Pradesh state archives

chapters.title: Opposition to the Simon Commission
chapters.html: The commission’s exclusion of Indian members provoked widespread protest. Police action injured Lala Lajpat Rai at Lahore; his death later in 1928 intensified nationalist anger. [27,33]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.caption: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: Saunders is killed
chapters.html: Bhagat Singh and his associates sought retaliation after Lajpat Rai’s death. They killed officer John Saunders, who was not their intended target, and linked the action to resistance against imperial violence. [33]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Bhagat Singh · 1929
image.caption: Historical photograph · Bhagat Singh · 1929
image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: Bombs in the Assembly
chapters.html: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly, circulated a leaflet and accepted arrest. People were injured; the defendants denied intending to kill and explained their political purpose. [33]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Bhagat Singh · 1929
image.caption: Historical photograph · Bhagat Singh · 1929
image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: Congress adopts complete independence
chapters.html: The Lahore Congress adopted complete independence as its goal. This moved its declared programme beyond earlier constitutional demands and prepared the ground for further collective action. [24,36]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.caption: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: A pledge to end British rule
chapters.html: The independence pledge presented British rule as a system to be ended. It connected the demand for freedom with a programme of disciplined collective action. [24,36]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1912
image.caption: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1912
image.author: Anonymous

chapters.title: Dandi challenges the salt monopoly
chapters.html: Gandhi marched to Dandi and broke the salt law. His letter to the viceroy set out grievances and planned civil disobedience, followed by salt campaigns across many regions. [36]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1930
image.caption: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1930
image.author: Anonymous

chapters.title: The salt campaign spreads
chapters.html: Protesters at Dharasana faced violent repression. Women participated prominently across the salt campaigns, extending civil disobedience far beyond Gandhi’s original marchers. [36]

image.alt: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.caption: Historic site · Sabarmati Ashram
image.author: Nizil Shah

chapters.title: The Chittagong armoury raids
chapters.html: Surya Sen’s revolutionaries attacked colonial armouries and communications. Fighting, underground resistance and trials followed; Kalpana Dutt’s later memoir records participants’ commitments, sacrifices and women’s involvement. [34]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Surya Sen
image.caption: Historical photograph · Surya Sen
image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: The Khudai Khidmatgars
chapters.html: Abdul Ghaffar Khan linked social reform and disciplined nonviolent resistance in the Frontier. Violence at Peshawar and the government’s military response brought the movement into the wider civil-disobedience struggle. [35]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The Round Table Conferences
chapters.html: Conferences in London debated constitutional arrangements while civil disobedience and repression continued. Representation, safeguards and the distribution of power remained subjects of profound disagreement. [27,36]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1931
image.caption: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1931
image.author: Anonymous

chapters.title: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact
chapters.html: The pact temporarily suspended civil disobedience and enabled Gandhi to attend the London conference. Negotiation did not immediately secure the independence demanded by the movement. [27,36]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1931
image.caption: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1931
image.author: Anonymous

chapters.title: Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev
chapters.html: The three revolutionaries were executed in March 1931. Their trial and prison writings widened political debate; Bhagat Singh’s address to young workers urged sustained organisation and social transformation. [33]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Bhagat Singh · 1929
image.caption: Historical photograph · Bhagat Singh · 1929
image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: The Poona Pact
chapters.html: Gandhi’s fast against separate electorates and Ambedkar’s negotiations produced reserved seats within joint electorates. The pact concerned caste and representation; Gandhi himself was not a signatory. [37]

image.alt: Historical photograph · B. R. Ambedkar and Rajendra Prasad · 1949
image.caption: Historical photograph · B. R. Ambedkar and Rajendra Prasad · 1949
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: Provincial autonomy with imperial safeguards
chapters.html: The Government of India Act created a wider framework for provincial autonomy. Major imperial safeguards and powers remained, setting limits on what elected Indian governments could do. [27]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.caption: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: Indian parties enter office
chapters.html: Elections brought Congress ministries to several provinces and strengthened other organisations elsewhere. Governing created opportunities and disputes over minorities, workers, cultivators and the limits of colonial autonomy. [27]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.caption: Historical photograph · The first Indian National Congress session · 1885
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: India enters the Second World War
chapters.html: The viceroy announced India’s participation without a sovereign Indian decision. Congress ministries resigned, while leaders and parties took different positions on the war and India’s political future. [27,40]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: The Lahore Resolution
chapters.html: The Muslim League called for arrangements involving independent states in Muslim-majority areas, with minority safeguards. Its wording records the League’s position in 1940, before subsequent negotiations and conflict. [39]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Individual satyagraha
chapters.html: Gandhi chose limited individual protest against restrictions on political speech and opposition to war. Vinoba Bhave was the first satyagrahi, followed by others into imprisonment. [38]

image.alt: Historic site · Mahatma Gandhi
image.caption: Historic site · Mahatma Gandhi
image.author: सुबोध कुलकर्णी

chapters.title: The Cripps proposals
chapters.html: Cripps offered a postwar constitutional process while reserving crucial wartime control. Congress, the League and other interests objected on different grounds, leaving fundamental disagreements unresolved. [40]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.date: 1942 onward · Mass mobilisation and underground resistance
chapters.title: The Quit India call
chapters.html: Congress demanded British withdrawal, and Gandhi called for disciplined nonviolent mass action. The arrest of national leaders was followed by a much more varied uprising and harsh repression. [38]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1946
image.caption: Historical photograph · Mahatma Gandhi · 1946
image.author: Max Desfor (1913- ) for Associated Press

chapters.title: An underground struggle continues
chapters.html: Aruna Asaf Ali, Usha Mehta and others sustained resistance. Strikes, demonstrations, underground organisation and attacks on communications followed the arrests, differing from the leadership’s stated nonviolent programme. [38]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.date: 1942–1945 · Southeast Asia and the northeastern frontier
chapters.title: The Indian National Army
chapters.html: The INA developed first under Mohan Singh and was reorganised under Subhas Chandra Bose with Japanese support. Its forces joined wartime campaigns towards India as another strategy for independence. [41]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Subhas Chandra Bose reviewing INA troops · 1940s
image.caption: Historical photograph · Subhas Chandra Bose reviewing INA troops · 1940s
image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: A provisional government and women soldiers
chapters.html: Bose proclaimed a provisional government in 1943. The Rani of Jhansi Regiment joined this military strategy for independence, which depended on Japanese support within Japan’s own imperial war. [41]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Captain Lakshmi Sahgal alongside Subhas Chandra Bose · 1940s
image.caption: Historical photograph · Captain Lakshmi Sahgal alongside Subhas Chandra Bose · 1940s
image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: Bengal’s wartime famine
chapters.html: Bengal’s famine killed on an enormous scale. Wartime demands, prices and failures of food access and administration compounded the crisis; the 1945 inquiry examined responsibility. [42]

image.alt: Map · The partition of Bengal · 1905
image.caption: Map · The partition of Bengal · 1905
image.author: XrysD

chapters.date: 1945–1946 · The Red Fort and public mobilisation
chapters.title: The INA trials
chapters.html: The trial of Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon prompted major mobilisation. Defence arguments challenged treating soldiers fighting for independence as ordinary offenders against British authority. [43]

image.alt: Historic site · Red Fort baoli, whose chambers held INA trial defendants · photographed in 2016
image.caption: Historic site · Red Fort baoli, whose chambers held INA trial defendants · photographed in 2016
image.author: Ramesh lalwani

chapters.title: The naval revolt
chapters.html: Naval ratings linked grievances over treatment and conditions with political demands. Civilian support, strikes, clashes and deaths followed; leading political organisations urged an end to the revolt. [43]

image.alt: Historical photograph · B. C. Dutt
image.caption: Historical photograph · B. C. Dutt
image.author: Government of India, Ministry of Culture (Amrit Mahotsav)

chapters.title: The Cabinet Mission plan
chapters.html: The mission proposed a union with limited central subjects, provincial groupings and a constituent assembly. Congress-League disagreements over authority and grouping undermined efforts to secure a common settlement. [40]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Communal violence spreads
chapters.html: Direct Action Day in Calcutta was followed by wider communal violence and retaliation. Fear, displacement and failures of protection eroded conditions for an agreed transfer of power. [40,44]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Refugees during Partition · 1947
image.caption: Historical photograph · Refugees during Partition · 1947
image.author: Photo Division, Government of India

chapters.title: Attlee announces a deadline
chapters.html: On 20 February 1947, Attlee announced transfer of power no later than June 1948. The commitment followed failed constitutional agreement amid overlapping political, military and financial pressures. [40]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The Constituent Assembly at independence · 1947
image.caption: Historical photograph · The Constituent Assembly at independence · 1947
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: The 3 June plan
chapters.html: Partition became the framework for transfer of power. Provincial decisions, boundary commissions and division of institutions, assets and armed forces proceeded under an accelerated timetable. [40,44]

image.alt: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.caption: Map · India in 1909, for geographical context · 1909
image.author: Oxford University Press

chapters.title: Two independent dominions
chapters.html: The Indian Independence Act set 15 August as the appointed day; British paramountcy ended. Pakistan held ceremonies on 14 August, and India’s Assembly met through the midnight transition. [44]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The Constituent Assembly at independence · 1947
image.caption: Historical photograph · The Constituent Assembly at independence · 1947
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: Partition’s human cost
chapters.html: The Radcliffe awards appeared on 17 August, after independence. Migration, killings, abductions and lost homes accompanied the borders; freedom did not immediately bring safety or recovery for displaced people. [44]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Refugees during Partition · 1947
image.caption: Historical photograph · Refugees during Partition · 1947
image.author: Photo Division, Government of India

chapters.title: India becomes a republic
chapters.html: The Constitution established the Republic in 1950. Integration and the distribution of rights remained major tasks, while some French and Portuguese territories still awaited the end of European rule. [45]

image.alt: Historical photograph · The Constituent Assembly at independence · 1947
image.caption: Historical photograph · The Constituent Assembly at independence · 1947
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: French settlements transfer in practice
chapters.html: The remaining French settlements underwent de facto transfer in 1954. Their change of administration continued territorial decolonisation after British rule had ended and the Republic had been established. [45]

image.alt: Map · Pondicherry and its surroundings
image.caption: Map · Pondicherry and its surroundings
image.author: Leveux, M.

chapters.title: Portuguese rule ends in Goa
chapters.html: Indian military action ended Portuguese rule in Goa in 1961. The end of this remaining colonial government marked another territorial stage beyond British withdrawal in 1947. [45]

image.alt: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.caption: Historic site · Portuguese Goa
image.author: Assamtimes

chapters.title: Legal transfer follows
chapters.html: The French settlements’ legal transfer followed in 1962, after the de facto transfer of 1954. British withdrawal, the Republic and these territorial changes were separate milestones of decolonisation. [45]

image.caption: Map · Pondicherry and its surroundings
image.author: Leveux, M.

story.sourcesHtml:
1. Anonymous, Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497–1499. Original manuscript and catalogue, Library of Congress. A Portuguese voyage account, used for the encounter with an already-established Indian Ocean commercial world and the arrival at Calicut; its judgments are those of the visiting expedition.

  2. Gaspar Correia, The Three Voyages of Vasco da Gama, and His Viceroyalty, translated by Henry E. J. Stanley, Hakluyt Society, 1869. The relevant part is the account of the second voyage and violence against shipping. Correia wrote later in the sixteenth century: this is an early Portuguese narrative, not a diary by a witness aboard the attacked pilgrim vessel.

  3. Afonso de Albuquerque and his son’s compilation, The Commentaries of the Great Afonso Dalboquerque, translated by Walter de Gray Birch, Hakluyt Society, 1875–1884; with Albuquerque’s correspondence. Digitised edition, Spanish National Research Council. Campaigns at Goa and the wider maritime strategy. The compilation’s purpose was to record and defend Albuquerque’s career.

  4. Francis Xavier, letters from Portuguese Asia, especially his appeals to João III during the 1540s, reproduced in Henry James Coleridge, The Life and Letters of St. Francis Xavier, 1872–1881. The letters are missionary testimony; the later editor’s biography is distinguished from those original documents.

  5. East India Company charters, diplomatic journals and correspondence. British Library, charters collection IOR/A/1; Thomas Roe’s Embassy to the Court of the Great Mogul, 1615–1619, edited by William Foster; Foster’s The English Factories in India, 1618–1669 (digitised document calendar); and company records reproduced in C. R. Wilson’s The Early Annals of the English in Bengal and Old Fort William in Bengal. These are different documentary series, used for the charter, settlements, permissions, conflicts and privileges. The British Library notes that the original 1600 charter is lost and survives through a contemporary transcript.

  6. VOC charter of 1602 and the Tranquebar agreement of 1620. Dutch company privileges are read as a European grant of corporate powers, not as Indian consent to overseas sovereignty. For Tranquebar, see the treaty reproduced with Jon Ólafsson’s account, National and University Library of Iceland, digitised edition, and the surviving treaty document.

  7. French East India Company correspondence and Robert Orme, A History of the Military Transactions of the British Nation in Indostan, 1763–1778. Original company correspondence and a contemporary British military history provide competing European perspectives on Pondicherry and the Carnatic conflicts. Orme’s interpretation is the British company’s side of the struggle, not an account representing every Indian participant.

  8. Robert Clive’s correspondence and his parliamentary evidence and defence in 1772–1773. These are used for the company’s Bengal operations and Clive’s account of its political arrangements. His explanations were delivered amid investigation of his conduct and are not treated as disinterested descriptions of conquest.

  9. Treaty texts collected in C. U. Aitchison, A Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads Relating to India and Neighbouring Countries, relevant volumes and revised editions. The documents include the 1765 arrangements, the Treaty of Salbai and treaties imposing subsidiary obligations. The Mewar treaty of 13 January 1818, articles 2–9 illustrates protection combined with supremacy and financial obligations. The later collection is a source for the actual instruments; the collector’s imperial classifications are not adopted as a measure of legitimacy.

  10. British parliamentary statutes: the Regulating Act (1773), Pitt’s India Act (1784), and the Charter Acts of 1813 and 1833, as originally enacted. These are the legal instruments for changes in company supervision and commercial privileges. They express the British legislature’s claims and arrangements, not the agreement of the governed populations.

  11. Land-revenue instruments and parliamentary evidence: Bengal Regulation I of 1793, the Fifth Report of the House of Commons Select Committee on the East India Company, 28 July 1812, and the later Select Committee evidence and revenue minutes of the 1820s–1830s. Fifth Report, digitised-edition catalogue; government reproduction of the Bengal Permanent Settlement Regulation. These records underlie the discussion of diwani administration, the 1770 crisis and differing revenue systems; later editorial explanations are separated from the original evidence.

  12. Tipu Sultan’s letters and British military dispatches. William Kirkpatrick, Select Letters of Tippoo Sultan (1811), digitised text, and Arthur Wellesley’s Indian correspondence in The Dispatches of Field Marshal the Duke of Wellington, edited by John Gurwood. Used for Mysore, alliance politics and later Maratha campaigns. Kirkpatrick’s translation and selection were produced after British conquest and require comparison with other evidence.

  13. Regional resistance: preserved official correspondence and proclamations. Southern campaign correspondence in Wellesley’s dispatches and Madras government records for the poligars and Malabar; Odisha State Archives, The Paika Rebellion: A Documentary Study (2017), reproducing earlier archival documents; and colonial correspondence and reports on the Kol uprising, also discussed in the administrative record identified in source 25. These records are used as the authorities’ evidence about the conflicts, not as unmediated accounts by every resisting community.

  14. Social policy and labour documents: Bengal Regulation XVII of 1829 on sati; Rammohan Roy’s contemporary writings and petitions on the practice; Macaulay’s Minute of 2 February 1835, original document reproduced by the National Archives of India; and nineteenth-century indenture contracts and official inquiries preserved in the Indian Immigration Archives, Mahatma Gandhi Institute. These different documents reveal legal programmes, Indian arguments and the terms and investigation of colonial labour migration.

  15. Dalhousie’s minutes, annexation proclamations and parliamentary papers, including the Punjab settlement, succession cases and Papers Relating to Oude (1856). These are original statements and official records explaining British decisions; allegations of misgovernment remain the annexing government’s justification, not a finding accepted on its authority alone.

  16. Official correspondence on the Santal uprising, 1855, including A. C. Bidwell’s letters and government proclamations, documentary extracts, suppression correspondence, August–September 1855. The language and priorities are those of officers trying to suppress the Hul; the source does not recover the whole range of Santal voices.

  17. Rebel proclamations of 1857–1858, including the Azamgarh Proclamation of 25 August 1857 (reproduced text) and Begum Hazrat Mahal’s response to Victoria’s proclamation. Authorship and English transmission of the Azamgarh text require care. The dated proclamations preserve particular rebel claims and constituencies, not a common programme unanimously held throughout the uprising.

  18. Contemporary campaign dispatches and participants’ testimony on 1857–1858: Hugh Rose’s Central India dispatches; government correspondence preserved in the Bihar State Archives’ digitised independence collection; and Edward Vibart, The Sepoy Mutiny as Seen by a Subaltern (1898). Dispatches are the military authorities’ record; Vibart’s later memoir is participant recollection. These different source types are distinguished when discussing campaigns and atrocities.

  19. Government of India Act 1858 and Victoria’s proclamation of 1 November 1858. Original proclamation, Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 2935014.a. The proclamation is cited for the promises it made, not as proof of their subsequent fulfilment.

  20. Indigo Commission evidence and official correspondence, 1860–1861. Original parliamentary papers reproducing the correspondence and the Bengal government’s minute. The commission record and cultivator evidence are a basis for examining coercion, refusal and the government’s response.

  21. Dadabhai Naoroji, Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901), digitised primary text, and his Congress presidential address of 1906. These are Naoroji’s own economic and political arguments, with his calculations identified as arguments open to examination.

  22. Indian Famine Commission reports, 1880 and 1901, and parliamentary and official evidence on railway finance and famine administration. These are among the original government inquiry reports in the National Archives of India’s commission collection. They are used for what officials investigated and recommended, alongside the contemporary criticism in source 21.

  23. Vernacular Press Act 1878 and contemporary press controversy; Tilak’s statements and the record of his 1908 sedition trial. Statutory provisions, contemporary journalism and trial statements record the conflict over publication and political criticism. Colonial criminal classifications are attributed to the authorities applying them.

  24. Indian National Congress reports and resolutions, including the sessions of 1885, 1906, 1907, 1916, 1920, 1923 and 1929, and the documents reproduced in the Maharashtra Government’s Source Material for a History of the Freedom Movement, volume II. The volume’s contents identify the original session reports, correspondence and resolutions; these separate documents are used for successive programmes and organisational disputes.

  25. Bihar and Orissa District Gazetteers: Ranchi (1917), administrative history and the account of Birsa’s movement, with the earlier official reports it draws upon. This is a colonial-period administrative compilation, not a statement by Birsa or an eyewitness diary of the 1831–1832 uprising. Its retrospective and adversarial character is retained when using its factual outline.

  26. Ghadar newspaper and the Sedition Committee report. Punjabi issue of 23 December 1913, original newspaper facsimile; Sedition Committee, Report (1918), digitised original. The newspaper supplies a revolutionary publication’s voice; the report supplies the state’s case for repression. Neither substitutes for the other.

  27. Constitutional statutes and official proceedings: the Indian Councils Act 1909, Government of India Acts 1919 and 1935, Montagu’s declaration of 20 August 1917, and the Indian Statutory Commission report (1930). The original laws and parliamentary and conference records are used for representation, dyarchy, provincial autonomy and the Simon Commission dispute. The UK Parliament’s historic debates preserve the government’s statements and contemporary challenges to them.

  28. M. K. Gandhi, Hind Swaraj (1909) and An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth (serialised 1925–1929), especially the chapters on Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda. Authoritative works collection, Gandhi Heritage Portal. The autobiography is Gandhi’s later account of his own campaigns; it is not treated as an independent record of every participant’s experience.

  29. Gandhi’s dated statements, Young India articles and trial statement, 1919–1922, in the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi. Collected Works collection record; original collected texts on satyagraha and non-cooperation. Used for his explanation of Rowlatt satyagraha, non-cooperation, Chauri Chaura and constructive work, rather than as evidence that every local action followed his instructions.

  30. Disorders Inquiry Committee report and evidence (1920), including Dyer’s testimony; Rabindranath Tagore’s letter renouncing his knighthood, 31 May 1919. The official inquiry and Tagore’s own letter are different primary responses to the Punjab violence. The report’s majority and Indian members’ conclusions should not be collapsed into a single unanimous finding.

  31. R. H. Hitchcock, A History of the Malabar Rebellion, 1921 (1925), and Gandhi’s contemporary comments on the Moplahs, including his Young India discussion of 20 October 1921. Hitchcock writes from the policing side; Gandhi’s comments are those of a political participant responding to the reports available to him. Allegations and assessments require attribution, including when discussing religious coercion and repression.

  32. Ram Prasad Bismil’s prison autobiography (1927) and the original Kakori prosecution and judgment record. These preserve a participant’s account and the colonial criminal case as different sources. The account identifies both the revolutionary purpose claimed for the action and the passenger’s death, without treating the prosecution’s interpretation as the only possible political description.

  33. Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt’s own documents: Assembly leaflet, 8 April 1929, joint court statement, June 1929, and To Young Political Workers, 2 February 1931. These are read with the Lahore prosecution record for the Saunders case and executions. The dated writings preserve political arguments that cannot be reduced to the acts of violence alone.

  34. Kalpana Dutt, Chittagong Armoury Raiders: Reminiscences (People’s Publishing House, 1945), original edition record, alongside the Chittagong proceedings. A participant memoir written later, not a claim that the author personally witnessed every action of the 1930 raid.

  35. Abdul Ghaffar Khan’s participant accounts and British records of Peshawar, 1930. Parliamentary statement of 14 May 1930 and questions on the Peshawar disturbances, 30 June 1930, compared with Ghaffar Khan’s My Life and Struggle (1969). The latter is retrospective participant testimony; the parliamentary answers present the government’s version.

  36. Independence pledge (1930), Gandhi’s letter to Irwin (2 March 1930), salt-campaign correspondence and the Gandhi-Irwin agreement (1931). Original resolutions and letter extracts assembled by the Gandhi Heritage Portal. Used for the announced aims and course of civil disobedience, with original conference and government correspondence for the negotiations.

  37. The Poona Pact, 24 September 1932, and B. R. Ambedkar, What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables (1945), reproduced in Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, volume 9. Government of India’s Ambedkar works collection. The agreement’s terms and signatories are distinguished from Gandhi’s fast and Ambedkar’s later criticism of the surrounding political pressure.

  38. Congress’s Quit India resolution and Gandhi’s speech of 8 August 1942, together with his 1940–1941 statements on individual satyagraha, in the Collected Works. Original resolution and speech reproduced by Mani Bhavan. The final adopted resolution is distinguished from the earlier April draft. Official records and participants’ accounts of the subsequent movement record actions beyond the imprisoned leadership’s direct control.

  39. All-India Muslim League, Lahore Resolution and Jinnah’s presidential address, March 1940, reproduced among the documents in Ambedkar, Pakistan or the Partition of India (1945), author’s original work and reproduced documents. The text’s original constitutional language and safeguards are retained, without presenting subsequent developments as already settled in March 1940.

  40. British proposals and announcements, 1942–1947: Cripps’s draft declaration; the Cabinet Mission statement of 16 May 1946; Attlee’s 20 February 1947 statement (original parliamentary text); and the 3 June 1947 plan. The original documents are also represented in The National Archives’ independence document collection, 1940–1946 and 1947 collection. Archive teaching introductions are distinguished from the original documents they reproduce.

  41. Subhas Chandra Bose’s speeches and Proclamation of the Provisional Government of Azad Hind, 21 October 1943, with original INA and British military records. See the Japanese diplomatic file on the provisional government, JACAR Ref. B02032938600. His declarations are used as the political programme of the movement, while the campaign’s outcome and Japanese alliance require the military record as well. The INA’s initial organisation under Mohan Singh is distinguished from its later leadership under Bose.

  42. Famine Inquiry Commission, Report on Bengal (Government of India, 1945), digitised original, University of North Bengal repository. This is an official post-crisis inquiry, used for its evidence and policy findings; it does not supply a final uncontested modern mortality estimate.

  43. INA trial proceedings and Bhulabhai Desai’s defence argument, 1945; Royal Indian Navy records and participants’ accounts, 1946. Original annual naval report, British Library IOR/L/MIL/17/9/363, contemporary parliamentary statements, and B. C. Dutt’s later memoir, Mutiny of the Innocents (1971). Trial argument, official reporting and retrospective participant testimony have different purposes and are kept distinct.

  44. The legal transfer, assembly proceedings and Partition records: Indian Independence Act 1947, original text; the Constituent Assembly’s 14–15 August 1947 proceedings, official report; Jinnah’s address of 11 August 1947; the Radcliffe awards published 17 August 1947; and contemporary correspondence and survivor testimony. National Archives’ collection and original records. The appointed legal date and Pakistan’s transfer ceremonies are distinguished.

  45. Post-1947 instruments: the Constitution of India (adopted 1949, effective 1950), the Treaty of Cession of the French Establishments in India (1956, effective 1962), and the Twelfth and Fourteenth Constitutional Amendment Acts (1962) concerning Goa and the former French establishments. These are the legal sources for the closing epilogue, with the territorial transfers distinguished from the end of British rule in 1947.
